query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: At a moderate annealing temperature (350°C), limited diffusion preserves the metastable solid solution state—and its uniform distribution of Mg essential for passivation—for short durations (around 20 hours). However, prolonged exposure (approximately 100 hours) allows sufficient diffusion for the nucleation and growth of intermetallic phases (notably Mg2Si), which locally deplete Mg and other critical elements, degrading both corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state produced via rapid cooling.
generation.intervention: Implement two annealing schedules at 350°C: one for 20 hours (serving as the controlled comparison) and one for 100 hours to trigger significant intermetallic precipitation.
generation.conditions: Annealing at 350°C in an inert or controlled atmosphere, with the key variable being the time of exposure (20 hours versus 100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: Time-dependent nucleation and growth of intermetallic precipitates, predominantly forming as Mg2Si compounds. Minimal precipitation occurs at 20 hours, whereas substantial grain interior and boundary precipitation appear after 100 hours.
generation.mechanism: At 350°C, atomic diffusion is slow, allowing the metastable SS state to persist for short durations and maintain a homogeneous element distribution required for forming a protective passivating oxide film. Over extended exposure, diffusion enables Mg2Si (and related) intermetallics to nucleate—especially at energetically favorable sites—thus redistributing Mg and compromising the oxide film integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The 20-hour annealed samples will retain a uniform microstructure with negligible Mg2Si formation, preserving corrosion/oxidation resistance similar to the as-cast state. In contrast, the 100-hour samples will exhibit >20% increased intermetallic volume fraction (with identifiable Mg2Si) and a corresponding >20% increase in corrosion current densities and degraded oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, metastable solid solution, which exhibits optimal passivating behavior due to its homogeneous distribution of alloying elements.
generation.boundary: A critical exposure duration between 50 and 100 hours at 350°C marks the transition from negligible to significant intermetallic formation.
generation.uncertainty: Low-to-moderate; while the diffusion kinetics at 350°C are well predicted by TTT and CALPHAD analyses, minor compositional variations may shift the exact time threshold.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical Mg-containing HEA samples and anneal them at 350°C for 20 and 100 hours. Use TEM and XRD to quantify the formation of Mg2Si intermetallics, and perform corrosion (potentiodynamic polarization) and high-temperature oxidation tests (mass gain and oxide film quality analysis).
measurements: Oxide scale integrity (mass gain and morphology)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 100-hour annealed sample does not show a statistically significant increase in Mg2Si content (e.g., >20% increase) and corresponding degradation in corrosion/oxidation performance relative to the 20-hour annealed sample, the hypothesis is falsified.

The cooling rate of LR HEA is the highest, thus R, σ and γ′ phases are all inhibited in this condition; with the decrease of cooling rate, the R phase shows up in an AC sample. As for the solid-state transformation process, the cooling rate of the Q1 HEA is quite high, and σ phase was restrained under the rapid quenching condition. And actually, the γ′ phase is also inhibited when quenched in water. All the phases can be formed when the cooling rate is sufficiently low, which is similar to the equilibrium condition. The FC1 sample in this study proved this conclusion. Intermetallic compound-based phases were found at lower concentrations but still significantly higher than in the conventional aluminum alloys. Two invariant transformations were indicated for Al3.4Cu0.5Si0.2Zn0.5Mg0.2 alloy, with a BCC-A2 phase stable between 316–488 °C. papers.title: First principles-based design of lightweight high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Lightweight HEAs containing Al, Be, Mg, Ti with a substitution of Cu, Si, or Li
papers.approach: DFT calculations at 0 K and room temperature using a Grand Canonical Linear Programming method to compare formation energies and assess metastability versus compound segregation.
papers.findings: Among the studied systems, only the AlBeMgTiSi alloy is predicted to be energetically stable in a single solid solution state at room temperature, while alloys like AlBeMgTiCu and AlBeMgTiLi require specialized processing (e.g., rapid cooling) to freeze in a metastable SS state against segregation into intermetallic compounds.
papers.mechanism: The balance between configurational entropy (augmented by temperature) and the formation energy drives stabilization of the SS state; substitution of one element alters the free energy landscape, promoting or inhibiting compound formation.

papers.title: Modeling and Experimental Results of Selected Lightweight Complex Concentrated Alloys, before and after Heat Treatment.
papers.system: Al–Cu–Si–Zn–Mg and Al–Mn–Zn–Mg–Si alloys (lightweight, complex concentrated systems)
papers.approach: Combined CALPHAD modeling, solidification simulations, and heat-treatment experiments to probe phase evolution and the order of intermetallic precipitation during thermal processing.
papers.findings: Initially as-cast alloys contain largely solid solution phases with some intermetallic compounds. Upon heat treatment, diffusion‐driven transformations result in a higher fraction of intermetallic phases (e.g., Mg2Si, Al9Mn2Si) with invariant transformations at specific temperature ranges.
papers.mechanism: Thermally activated diffusion leads to nucleation and growth of intermetallic compound phases from the metastable solid solution as a function of temperature and composition, indicating a kinetic pathway that transitions from metastable SS to a multiphase equilibrium.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of MgTiZn and Mg₄TiZn Alloys After Ball Milling and Subsequent Spark Plasma Sintering.
papers.system: Mg–Ti–Zn alloys processed by high-energy ball milling and SPS
papers.approach: Synthesis via ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering, with microstructural characterization (XRD, TEM, SEM) and evaluation of corrosion performance (potentiodynamic polarization, immersion tests).
papers.findings: The MgTiZn (TZ) alloy develops a microstructure with abundant intermetallic phases (Ti2Zn, Mg21Zn25) and fine oxide particles, while Mg₄TiZn (4TZ) retains a more homogeneous Mg-rich matrix with solid solution domains. Both exhibit good corrosion resistance due to passivating surface film formation, particularly a TiO₂-rich layer in TZ.
papers.mechanism: The relative distribution and morphology of intermetallic compounds and solid solution domains promote the formation of protective oxides that passivate the surface. The processing methods refine the grain sizes and aid in achieving the metastable SS state that later evolves via diffusion-controlled precipitation.

papers.title: Kinetic ways of tailoring phases in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiTi₀.4 high-entropy alloy (as a model system for kinetic phase evolution)
papers.approach: Systematic investigation of phase selection via variations in cooling rate during both solidification and solid-state transformations, supported by CALPHAD modeling and kinetic analysis (CCT curves).
papers.findings: Rapid cooling (e.g., laser remelting) inhibits the formation of equilibrium intermetallic phases, preserving a metastable SS matrix. Slower cooling allows the nucleation of equilibrium phases such as σ, γ′, R, and Laves phases.
papers.mechanism: The kinetics of atomic diffusion and nucleation govern phase selection. The cooling rate sets the time available for diffusion, thus controlling whether intermetallic compounds form from the metastable SS state, highlighting a kinetic pathway independent of purely thermodynamic driving forces.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: High entropy alloys with multiple oxide-forming elements (including Mg-containing systems indirectly)
papers.approach: Combination of in situ atom probe tomography, high-resolution electron microscopy, and X-ray spectroscopy to analyze compositional and structural changes in oxide scales under high-temperature oxidation.
papers.findings: Oxide scale formation is strongly dependent on differential diffusion rates (e.g., Cr vs. O, Al₂O₃ formation) and complex interactions among the multiple elements present; the structure of the oxide film is key to oxidation resistance.
papers.mechanism: Competition between outward diffusion of reactive elements (like Cr) and inward oxygen diffusion determines the growth and stability of the oxide scale, with protective Al₂O₃ formation providing enhanced resistance. The evolution of intermetallics in the substrate could affect the availability of alloying elements that form these oxides.

established: Mg-containing lightweight HEAs can be processed to obtain a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution state using methods like rapid cooling and powder metallurgy.
Intermetallic compound formation is a common kinetic pathway in these alloys as they progress toward thermodynamic equilibrium during heat treatment or service exposure.
The corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance of these alloys are closely linked to the formation of passivating oxide films (e.g., TiO₂, Al₂O₃) that depend on the microstructural state.
Cooling rate and processing history strongly influence the balance between metastable SS retention and intermetallic precipitation.

approaches_tried.approach: Rapid solidification (fast cooling) to freeze in a metastable solid solution
approaches_tried.outcome: Preservation of a fine, supersaturated SS state with improved initial corrosion and oxidation resistance, but with inherent instability toward intermetallic precipitation upon subsequent thermal exposure.

approaches_tried.approach: Heat treatment (annealing) and controlled cooling (furnace cooling vs quenching) to study phase transformation kinetics
approaches_tried.outcome: Formation of equilibrium intermetallic phases from the metastable SS, with transformation kinetics influenced by cooling rate; altered corrosion/passivation behavior observed.

approaches_tried.approach: Ball milling combined with spark plasma sintering (SPS) to engineer microstructural refinement
approaches_tried.outcome: Production of Mg-containing alloys with refined grain structure and controlled intermetallic distribution, achieving improved corrosion resistance due to uniform passivating oxide layer formation.

mechanisms: Kinetics of diffusion-controlled intermetallic precipitation from a metastable solid solution state.
The competition between rapid cooling for SS retention and slower cooling allowing atomic rearrangements leading to intermetallic formation.
Formation of passivating oxide films (e.g., TiO₂, Al₂O₃) as influenced by the evolving microstructure and distribution of alloying elements.
disagreements: Some studies indicate that the presence of intermetallic compounds can enhance passivation by acting as barriers, while others suggest that intermetallic precipitation compromises corrosion resistance by creating micro-galvanic cells.
There is ongoing debate over whether kinetic effects (e.g., sluggish diffusion in HEAs) significantly alter transformation pathways relative to classical thermodynamic predictions.
open_questions: What is the precise transformation pathway and kinetics governing the evolution from a metastable SS state to a microstructure containing intermetallic compounds in Mg-containing lightweight HEAs?

How do microstructural changes (including intermetallic morphology and distribution) quantitatively affect the balance between corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation performance over extended service regimes?
What are the critical processing parameters that control the threshold between beneficial passivation and detrimental phase segregation?
opportunities: Designing controlled thermal exposure experiments comparing samples retained in the initial metastable SS state versus those intentionally aged to precipitate intermetallic compounds, with systematic evaluation of corrosion and oxidation behavior.
Combining rapid cooling with subsequent low-temperature annealing to fine-tune intermetallic precipitation kinetics and optimize passivating oxide film formation.

Exploring compositional modifications (e.g., slight adjustments in Mg, Ti, or Zn content) to modulate the competing kinetics and thermodynamic driving forces for intermetallic versus SS retention under service-regime boundaries (e.g., temperatures encountered in high-temperature oxidation)
Employing in situ characterization techniques (such as TEM, APT, and XPS) during controlled heat treatments to capture real-time evolution of phase transformations and oxide scale development.

directions.direction: Examine thermal activation effects on phase transformation by heat‐treatment to trigger diffusion‐driven intermetallic nucleation and growth from the metastable SS state.
directions.assessment: Directly targets the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics. This approach leverages known diffusion‐limitations and intermetallic precipitation phenomena in HEAs (e.g., PMC10728166 and PMC5043342), and it is feasible through controlled annealing experiments.

directions.direction: Investigate the time–temperature dependency of the kinetic transformation via controlled annealing at moderate temperatures to separate early‐stage fine precipitation from later coarsening, and correlate these changes with corrosion/oxidation behavior.
directions.assessment: Addresses the transformation pathway by comparing short versus prolonged annealing. This method is supported by kinetic studies (e.g., PMC5043342 and PMC7579168) and is highly feasible with differential thermal analysis and corrosion testing.

directions.direction: Study the role of precipitate size and coherency using a two‐step annealing approach that first induces fine, coherent intermetallics then promotes coarsening, in order to understand how microstructure mediates passivating oxide film formation.
directions.type: Processing/Heat Treatment Coupled with Surface/Coating Properties
directions.assessment: Directly links the microstructural mediator (intermetallic precipitate size/coherency) with the protective passivating film. Supported by reports on oxide film formation dependence on microstructure (e.g., PMC12299034, PMC11169556), this study is experimentally accessible.

directions.direction: Alter the alloy’s free energy landscape via minor compositional tuning (e.g., small Si addition) to kinetically delay intermetallic precipitation, thereby preserving the metastable SS state and intact corrosion/oxidation properties.
directions.assessment: This strategy uses compositional modification to modulate the transformation kinetics. It respects material constraints and leverages theoretical insights (e.g., PMC10728166 and CALPHAD modeling from PMC7579168), while offering a controlled comparison between modified and unmodified alloys.

candidates.hypothesis: Controlled low-temperature annealing at 300°C for 50 hours induces the formation of fine, coherent intermetallic precipitates (with a critical size threshold near 50 nm) that promote uniform surface redistribution of key elements and foster a continuous, protective passivating oxide film. However, additional high-temperature exposure (450°C for another 50 hours) causes these precipitates to coarsen beyond the threshold, triggering micro-galvanic effects that deteriorate corrosion resistance.
candidates.intervention: Subject one set of samples to a single-step anneal at 300°C for 50 hours and a second set to a two-step treatment: first 300°C for 50 hours followed by 450°C for 50 hours.
candidates.changes: Integrated a theoretical basis for the critical precipitate size (around 50 nm) drawn from phase-field and TEM studies, and clarified the role of precipitate coherency in facilitating uniform oxide film formation while acknowledging that local alloy chemistry may adjust the exact threshold.

candidates.hypothesis: Thermal exposure at service-relevant temperatures (450°C for 100 hours) promotes diffusion-driven nucleation of intermetallic compounds—predominantly at high-energy grain boundaries—leading to localized depletion of passivating elements and resulting in a compromised oxide film, which in turn degrades corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance compared to the as-cast state.
candidates.intervention: Subject samples to a controlled heat treatment at approximately 450°C for 100 hours, with an otherwise identical, untreated sample serving as the comparison.
candidates.changes: Enhanced the discussion of grain boundary chemistry by specifying that high-angle grain boundaries promote the nucleation of intermetallic phases (such as Mg2X compounds), and clarified that these localized precipitates deplete passivating elements. Added explicit mention of the role of grain boundary structure in facilitating diffusion-driven transformations.

candidates.hypothesis: A minor compositional modification by incorporating approximately 1–2 at.% Si into the Mg-containing HEA increases the nucleation barrier for intermetallic compounds by subtly altering the free energy landscape. This kinetic delay maintains the metastable solid solution state, preserving uniform passivating oxide film formation and superior corrosion/oxidation resistance compared to an otherwise identical unmodified alloy.
candidates.intervention: Expose both alloy variants to an identical thermal treatment regimen, for instance, 400°C for 100 hours, under a controlled atmosphere.
candidates.changes: Reconciled the apparent conflict regarding Si addition by emphasizing that a minor addition (1–2 at.%) is applied in the dilute limit. Provided additional mechanistic detail on how such a Si addition increases diffusion barriers and alters the free energy landscape—based on first principles—to delay intermetallic nucleation without reducing the FCC solid solution fraction.
